While I think nuclear power will be necessary to moving us away from fossil fuels, it's hard to look at Fukishima, Chernobyl, and the long lasting environmental consequences of the occasional meltdown and not worry about nuclear power's unintended side effects.

Just for fun, compare it to the death toll and environmental consequences of fossil fuels. It's a lot like comparing the safety of flying and driving.

Oh, and Chernobyl isn't really fair. It was built in 1972 and had design issues before they moved the first shovel full of dirt. Modern plants can be built that are just fantastically safe. Anyone that claims to care about the environment should be pushing hard for fission.

Some of that difference is due to how much of each we use though. Our environment has limits, and when we consume less than the limit it has basically no effect, but when we go over the limit the problems we cause tend to grow rapidly and cause other problems. If we cut fossil fuel use so our greenhouse gas emissions dropped to below the sustainable limit, we wouldn't just do less damage overall, we'd do less environmental damage per unit of energy created by fossil fuel use. Similarly, the occasional nuclear disaster or contaminated nuclear waste site may have only a small radius of effect or (as in Fukishima's case) spread a small amount of damage over a wide area that can handle it. However, if we were producing 10 times as much nuclear power and those events were much more frequent, how many Fukishimas would it take to wipe out aquatic species with low radiation resistance? How soon after that would the negative feedback loops start kicking in and compounding the damage? How would more widespread habitat destruction from radiation put pressure on the rest of the ecosystem?

It might still turn out to be less dangerous than fossil fuels (not saying it isn't), but there are problems with every kind of energy we produce and those problems get worse the more of it you produce. The real solution isn't just switching energy types (even hydro, wind, and solar cause some wildlife loss and habitat contamination from mining the metals to build the turbines/solar panels). The real solution is an economic shift that rejects welfare, stimulus spending, and other policies that encourage excessive consumption.
